newsitem.title: UK: West condemns Serbia over human rights.
newsitem.headline: West condemns Serbia over human rights.

text.p: The United States and Western allies on Wednesday made a strong attack on Serbia, which has shut down an independent radio station after huge street protests against alleged ballot rigging.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum, President Bill Clinton's envoy to former Yugoslavia, said the state of democracy in Serbia was "deplorable".
U.S. relations with Belgrade would remain frosty until Serbia's democratic record improved.

"We believe that both in the treatment of elections and political parties, also the state of the media there, the overall democratic process in Serbia really is in a very sad state," Kornblum told reporters.
Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said: "We are increasingly concerned about events in Serbia because they obviously have profound implications for the peace process."
Concern was also expressed by the European Union and by the international community's envoy in Bosnia, Carl Bildt.
The comments came during a conference being held to review the peace process 12 months after the Dayton peace accord which ended 43 months of war in Bosnia.
The Bosnia conference has been overshadowed by events in Belgrade, where the opposition and student supporters have held 17 days of demonstrations in protest at the outcome of local elections.

A Belgrade court on Wednesday rejected a complaint by Serbia's Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling socialists had rigged last month's election results to deprive it of victory in Belgrade.
About 100 demonstrators gathered outside the London conference venue, waving banners saying: "Kick Milosevic Out".
Kornblum called on Belgrade to improve its human rights record: "It must open the political process. It must allow for freedom of opinion and more diversity of political view."
Despite its condemnation of Milosevic's actions, the United States has stopped short of seeking to re-impose the full trade sanctions against Belgrade that the United Nations removed last year.
Instead Washington wants to maintain an "outer wall" of American sanctions against Belgrade.
Kornblum said: "We will continue to do that and we will continue to restrict any kind of development with Serbia until there is movement on democratic devlopment."
Kornblum's condemnation of Belgrade's human rights record was echoed by other Western leaders.
Bildt said a tragedy was unfolding in Belgrade.
"Today the forces of repression and retrogression seem to be gaining the upper hand in the regime in Belgrade."
The EU presidency, held by Ireland, condemned the closure of Radio B-92, an independent Belgrade station which had been reporting on anti-Milosevic demonstrations.
The EU noted "with dismay that the Serb authorities seem determined to ignore calls from the international community...for the full observance of international democratic principles".
